title: Unique Paths
interviewTips: Ask about constraints and overflow: m,n <= 100 fits in 32-bit answer but factorials overflow, so need iterative multiply-divide or long.
Trade-off: DP is extensible to obstacles and is expected follow-up to Unique Paths II, while combinatorics is O(1) space but only works for empty grid.
Edge-case tip: single row or single column always has 1 path, including m=1, n=1; confirm movement is only right and down.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Recursion
approaches.intuition: From each cell you can only go right or down. Try both choices recursively and sum the number of ways to reach the target. Base case is reaching bottom-right which counts as 1 path.
approaches.theory: This explores the full binary decision tree of moves. At each cell (r,c) the count is f(r,c) = f(r+1,c) + f(r,c+1). It is correct by exhaustive enumeration but recomputes overlapping subproblems many times, leading to exponential time.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each cell branches into 2 calls and path length is m+n-2, so number of recursive calls is exponential in grid size.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Recursion stack depth equals max path length m+n-2 for down plus right moves.

steps: start at (0,0), branch down to (1,0) and right to (0,1)

edgeCases: m=1, n=1 returns 1, base case immediately hit
m=1 or n=1 returns 1, only one straight line path
TLE for m,n > ~15 due to exponential blowup

approaches.name: Approach 2: Dynamic Programming with 1D Array
approaches.intuition: Number of ways to reach a cell is sum of ways from top and left. First row and first column are all 1 because there is only one straight path. Fill row by row reusing one array.
approaches.theory: Optimal substructure: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] with dp[0][*]=dp[*][0]=1. Since current row only needs previous row, compress to 1D: dp[j] += dp[j-1] where dp[j] holds previous row value before update and dp[j-1] holds current row value. Iterate m-1 times over n columns.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of m*n cells computed once with O(1) addition.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only one row of size n stored; can also use O(min(m,n)) by iterating over smaller dimension.

edgeCases: m=1 or n=1 returns 1 without loop execution
m=100, n=100 fits in 32-bit signed int, no overflow in DP addition
Large m with small n still efficient if you choose dimension min for array size

approaches.name: Approach 3: Combinatorics Formula
approaches.intuition: Every path needs exactly m-1 downs and n-1 rights in any order, total N=m+n-2 moves. Choosing positions of downs (or rights) among N determines the path. Answer is binomial coefficient C(N, min(m-1,n-1)).
approaches.theory: Number of sequences with m-1 D and n-1 R is N choose m-1 = N! / ((m-1)! (n-1)!). Compute iteratively as res = product_{i=1..k} (N-k+i)/i with k=min(m-1,n-1) to keep intermediate divisible and avoid factorial overflow. Division at each step is exact, using 64-bit for safety.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single loop of k = min(m-1,n-1) iterations with O(1) multiply and divide.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only a few integer variables used.

edgeCases: m=1 or n=1 gives N=m+n-2, k=0, loop skipped, returns 1
Avoid computing factorials directly to prevent overflow; multiply then divide each iteration
